titre: Mellanby's Dog Didn't Discover Vitamin D
accroche: In 1919, cod liver oil cures a dog's rickets. Mellanby credits vitamin A. He's wrong.
contenu_vulgarise:
In London, in 1918, a physiologist keeps puppies away from sunlight and feeds them a porridge of cereal, milk, and salt. Within a few weeks, their legs bow and their joints swell: a rickets nearly identical to the one afflicting children in England's industrial slums. Edward Mellanby then adds cod liver oil to the ration of some of the puppies. Their bones straighten out. He has proof that rickets comes from diet, not from a lack of fresh air or an infection, as was still widely believed.

## A Good Cure, a Wrong Explanation

Mellanby publishes his results on March 15, 1919, as two lectures delivered at the Royal College of Surgeons and reprinted in The Lancet. He offers an explanation: cod liver oil works because it contains vitamin A, the only known fat-soluble dietary factor at the time, identified a few years earlier by the American chemist Elmer McCollum. The explanation holds up: cod liver oil is, after all, the richest known source of vitamin A, and nothing in Mellanby's experiment forces anyone to look further. The cure he proposes is the right one. The cause he gives it is not.

## McCollum Takes Vitamin A Out of the Equation

In 1922, McCollum repeats the experiment with a decisive twist. His team bubbles hot air through cod liver oil for several hours. This aeration destroys the vitamin A activity: rats fed this oil stop growing and develop the eye lesions typical of vitamin A deficiency. But given to rachitic dogs, the same aerated oil still cures their bones. If vitamin A is destroyed and rickets still heals, the cure cannot be coming from vitamin A. McCollum publishes the demonstration in volume 53 of the Journal of Biological Chemistry, pages 293 to 312, and names the responsible substance vitamin D: the fourth vitamin identified, after A, B, and C. The following year, two independent teams each confirm the result on their own.

## The Shift

The story is often told as if Mellanby discovered vitamin D by curing dogs. The episode actually separates two things people conflate: having the right cure, and having the right explanation. Mellanby had the first; McCollum supplied the second, by deliberately destroying what Mellanby believed was the active cause, to see whether the effect survived without it. A solid experimental result, cod liver oil cures rickets, carried a false theory for three years, because no one had needed to put it to the test: it already explained everything that had been observed. This isn't a fault peculiar to Mellanby. It's what any explanation does once it hasn't yet been proven wrong: it stops being questioned the moment it stops surprising.

repere.texte: McCollum publishes his demonstration in volume 53 of the Journal of Biological Chemistry, pages 293 to 312: aerated cod liver oil, stripped of its vitamin A activity, still cures a dog's rickets. He names the responsible substance vitamin D, the fourth vitamin identified.
repere.source: McCollum, E.V., Simmonds, N., Becker, J.E., Shipley, P.G., Journal of Biological Chemistry, vol. 53, 1922, pp. 293-312

carte.punch: Mellanby didn't discover vitamin D. He cured rickets for the wrong reason.
carte.idee: In 1919, Mellanby cures a dog's rickets with cod liver oil and credits the effect to vitamin A. In 1922, McCollum destroys the vitamin A in that same oil: it still cures. The active substance is different; he names it vitamin D.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Elmer McCollum, the Chemist Who Had Named Vitamin A
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Biography of the chemist who identified vitamin A in 1913-1915, before showing in 1922 that it didn't explain the cure for rickets.

quiz.question: Why wasn't Mellanby's 1919 experiment on dogs enough to identify vitamin D?
choix: Because cod liver oil didn't cure rickets in all the dogs tested
Because his results were never published in a scientific journal
Because he credited the curative effect to vitamin A, already known, rather than to a distinct substance
Because he had only tested cod liver oil on rats, never on dogs
quiz.explication: The oil did cure the dogs, and Mellanby published the work in The Lancet in 1919. His mistake lies in the cause: he credits it to vitamin A, already identified, when McCollum will show in 1922 that it is a distinct substance, named vitamin D.
